name: Rectangle 9
text: Why is the problem challenging?
Simplify without distorting
An analogy must preserve the cookie’s purpose.
Handle uncertain purposes
Missing declarations limit what we can explain.
Interpret ambiguous answers
“Is this tracking me?” is a question, not consent.
Make engagement useful
Enjoyment must lead to better understanding.
The design must preserve meaning and the user’s intended choice.

The problem involves more than replacing technical terms with pictures. First, an analogy can simplify a request but must not misrepresent its purpose or safety. Second, cookie metadata alone does not establish purpose; public declarations can be incomplete or stale. Third, a question or an uncertain response must not be treated as permission. Clarify before applying a decision. Finally, engagement is useful only if users understand requests and retain control. Enjoyment alone cannot establish that consent is informed. Sources: project report, Chapters 2, 4 and 5; src/engine/input-adapter.js, src/engine/rules.js and server.js. These are design challenges, not claimed user-study findings.

title: How each feature addresses the problem

name: Rectangle 9
text: How each feature addresses the problem
Each feature has a proposed benefit to evaluate
Evaluate understanding, choice accuracy, effort and engagement.

preview: User difficulty | Design response | Intended benefit

text: This maps the user problem to each implemented design feature and its intended benefit. The benefits are hypotheses for evaluation. The home and guest analogy explains purpose; the technical details remain inspectable. Concrete scenarios make requests easier to relate to personal preferences. The chatbot provides a way to ask questions and clarify ambiguous answers, but it introduces interpretation risk, so structured decisions are validated by the rules engine. Progress feedback is intended to sustain attention; measure whether it helps without adding too much effort. Purpose evidence and uncertainty labels let users see limits rather than assume all purposes are verified. For each feature, gather task measures and participant explanations. Source: report Sections 2.2–2.3, Chapter 4 and Chapter 5; current prototype code.

name: Rectangle 9
text: The research gap
Existing work

Consent interface studies explain how design affects choices.
CookieBlock classifies cookies and enforces preferences.
Gap in reviewed work

The reviewed works do not evaluate this gamified journey.
Its effect on understanding and choice accuracy is untested.
Our contribution

A working Cookie Homes prototype and a planned
comparison with conventional consent controls.
This gap is scoped to the reviewed works; effectiveness remains to be tested.

Define the gap with reference to the reviewed works. Nouwens et al. study how consent interface design affects decisions. CookieBlock classifies cookies and enforces user preferences; its classification approach does not evaluate this project’s conversational home and guest journey. Cookie Homes asks how users understand requests and express the preferences that consent mechanisms act on. The contribution is the designed and implemented interaction plus a planned evaluation of understanding, fidelity to intent, usability and engagement. Do not claim that no gamified privacy system exists or that effectiveness has already been established. Sources: Nouwens, M., Liccardi, I., Veale, M., Karger, D. and Kagal, L. (2020). Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence. CHI. https://doi.org/10.1145/3313831.3376321 ; Bollinger, D., Kubicek, K., Cotrini, C. and Basin, D. (2022). Automating Cookie Consent and GDPR Violation Detection. USENIX Security. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity22/presentation/bollinger ; project report Chapters 3–5.
